en: Imagine this. It happens to many middle class families in India.
visual: Night, an Indian hospital lobby: slow push in on a tired man on a steel bench, a medical file on his knees (REAL b-roll, ILLUSTRATIVE FOOTAGE).
sound: Hospital room tone, a distant PA chime
pacing: Cold open, no music for 2 s; small logo bug from 0:02

en: You pay thirty five thousand rupees every year for health insurance. You renew it on time for six straight years. You never miss a single payment.
visual: Six premium receipts slide into a stack, a year stamp on each (SIMULATION); counter ticks up in the lower corner.

en: Then, an emergency. Your father is admitted to the hospital.
visual: Real b-roll: stretcher wheeled through hospital doors; corridor lights streak overhead.

en: Three days later, it is nine o'clock at night. You are standing at the billing counter. The discharge papers are ready. The bill is four and a half lakh rupees.
visual: Billing counter at night, printer pushing out a long bill; macro on the total (SIMULATION bill, no real hospital name).

en: The man at the desk hands you one printed letter. It says, sorry sir, your cashless request is denied. Reason, non disclosure of a pre existing disease.
visual: Macro: a letter slides across the counter; red stamp CASHLESS DENIED lands on it (SIMULATION, film motif).

en: Your heart drops. Your family panics.
visual: Real b-roll: a woman's hands tighten on a dupatta in a waiting room; shallow focus.

en: It is night. The banks are closed. You break your fixed deposit, borrow from relatives, or swipe a credit card, just to take your father home.
visual: Fast three-shot montage: phone banking screen (SIMULATION), a phone call in a corridor, a card tapped on a hospital POS machine (REAL b-roll).

en: And you ask, why did I pay all these years, if they leave me alone the one time I need them?
visual: Slow push on the man on the bench, now alone; the red stamp reflected in the glass door.
sound: Music drops to a single held note

en: Here is the truth. In most cases like this, the door is not closed. A cashless denial is not a claim rejection. And after five years of policy, there is a rule that stops this exact excuse.
visual: The red CASHLESS DENIED stamp cracks; a cyan overstamp lands: NOT A CLAIM REJECTION (film motif, thumbnail promise by 0:30).
onscreen: NOT A CLAIM REJECTION [IRDAI MASTER CIRCULAR | 29 MAY 2024]
sound: 1.5 s music silence, then low braam

en: Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore.
visual: Logo sting (assets/brand), cyan light sweep.
pacing: Name spoken: logo sting, not the bug

en: In this video, we will not shout, and we will not sell you any policy. We will read the real IRDAI rules, see who really says no, and learn the step by step way to get your money back.
visual: Desk top shot: an IRDAI circular printout and a hospital bill side by side under a desk lamp; camera slides across (REAL props or credited PDF render).
sound: Investigative synth bed enters at −25 dB

en: Let us break it down in simple words.
visual: Whip transition into the chapter card: 2-word chapter title in a lower third over corridor footage (no full-screen card).

en: First, who actually says no to you at the hospital desk?
visual: Real b-roll: an insurance or TPA help desk inside an Indian hospital; staff at computers.

en: Most people think the insurance company itself is checking your reports. But usually, the papers go to a middleman called a TPA. Third Party Administrator.
visual: Animated flow (HyperFrames, SVG/GSAP): PATIENT → HOSPITAL → TPA → INSURANCE COMPANY, files travelling along the arrows; TPA node glows amber.
sound: Soft data ticks on each arrow

en: Many think a TPA is a neutral government doctor. It is not. A TPA is a private company. The insurance company hires it and pays it, to process your claim papers.
visual: Split screen: left, red-tinted myth tag 'NEUTRAL GOVT DOCTOR?' crossed out; right, cyan document card quoting the IRDAI TPA rule.
onscreen: MYTH · NEUTRAL GOVT DOCTOR ✕ [IRDAI (TPA – HEALTH SERVICES) REGULATIONS]

en: IRDAI even says the TPA's pay cannot depend on how much claim money gets paid out. But here is the part most people never hear.
visual: Forensic magnifier over the master circular line on TPA remuneration; highlighter swipe.

en: Under IRDAI rules, no claim can be rejected without the approval of the insurance company's own claims review committee. And if they reject it, fully or partly, they must tell you the exact policy clause.
visual: Highlighter on para 17(a) and 17(b) of the circular (credited PDF, magnifier).
onscreen: REJECTION NEEDS COMMITTEE APPROVAL [IRDAI MASTER CIRCULAR | PARA 17]

en: So, a cashless no at the desk only means one thing. The company did not agree to pay the hospital directly, at that moment. Your right to claim the money is still alive.
visual: The red stamp from H005 again; it fades to grey while a cyan line reads REIMBURSEMENT STILL OPEN.

en: Now, the three reasons you will see most often on these letters.
visual: Three case-file tabs slide in from the right, numbered 1 2 3 (kinetic accent in lower third).

en: Reason number one. Non disclosure of a pre existing disease.
visual: Tab 1 opens: SIMULATION denial letter, the phrase highlighted.

en: Say you were admitted for a broken leg, or dengue. A junior doctor writes one line in your notes. Patient has mild blood pressure.
visual: Real b-roll: leg in a cast / dengue ward; then macro on handwritten case notes (SIMULATION notes) as a pen writes 'k/c/o mild HTN'.

en: The reviewer sees that one line. He opens your proposal form from five years ago, and says, you did not declare blood pressure. Cashless denied.
visual: Animated: a highlighter finds the line in the notes, a dotted line jumps back to an old proposal form with an empty tick box (SIMULATION).

en: Many families ask, does blood pressure cause a broken leg? It does not. But in the first five years of your policy, the company can still raise this question. After five years, the rule changes. We will come to that.
visual: Leg X-ray light box (REAL b-roll) next to a BP cuff; a small 5-YEAR ring appears and pulses once (sets up chapter 3).

en: Reason number two. Not medically necessary. They say your treatment could have been done without staying in hospital.
visual: Tab 2: SIMULATION letter phrase 'admission not justified'; real b-roll of an OPD queue.

en: Reason number three. Room rent limit, and proportionate deduction.
visual: Tab 3: a hospital room door with a price plate (SIMULATION).

en: Say your policy allows a room of five thousand rupees a day. But you took a room of eight thousand. They do not just cut the three thousand rupee difference.
visual: BOARD (video/lib/whiteboard): marker writes LIMIT 5,000 / ROOM 8,000 and circles the 3,000 gap.

en: They pay only five out of every eight rupees, on the surgery, doctor and nursing charges too. That is a cut of about thirty seven percent on those charges.
visual: BOARD: 5 ÷ 8 = 62.5%, then the cut applied to surgery, doctor and nursing lines; the total cut grows to about sixty thousand while the room difference was nine thousand.
onscreen: OUR CALCULATION · 37.5% CUT [IRDAI PRODUCT FILING GUIDELINES | 2020]
pacing: Let the maths breathe: 1 s hold on the total

en: One good thing. IRDAI does not allow this cut on medicines, implants, tests and ICU charges. Check your bill for that.
visual: BOARD: medicines, implants, tests, ICU written in a green column with a tick each.
onscreen: NO CUT · MEDICINES · IMPLANTS · TESTS · ICU

en: When a family sees these letters, they feel helpless. They think the door is closed forever.
visual: Real b-roll: an elderly couple in a hospital corridor at night; slow drift.

en: It is not. Here is the rule that protects you.
visual: Push into the IRDAI circular's cover page (credited PDF render) as the chapter lower third appears.

en: Now listen carefully. This may be the most important rule in health insurance.
visual: Desk lamp clicks on over the printed master circular; slow push.

en: It is called the moratorium period.
visual: Kinetic word MORATORIUM types on in a lower third, cyan.

en: Earlier, this period was eight years. In May twenty twenty four, IRDAI brought it down from eight years to five years.
visual: Animated calendar ring: 96 month segments, 36 fall away, 60 remain and glow cyan.

en: That means sixty months in a row, with no break in your policy.
visual: The 60-month ring fills month by month, a renewal tick on each year.

en: So what does it mean for you?
visual: Hold on the full ring; light sweeps across it.
pacing: VO_PAUSE 3.0 s after this line (owner's 3 s silence): the clause below fills the screen behind a magnifier

en: After five years of continuous cover, the company cannot question your policy or your claim, saying you did not disclose something, or you gave wrong details.
visual: Animated golden highlighter slides across the real clause text: 'No policy and claim of health insurance shall be contestable on any grounds of non-disclosure and/or misrepresentation except for established fraud, after the completion of the Moratorium Period, i.e. 60 months of continuous coverage'.
sound: 1.5 s total music silence before, low braam as the highlight completes

en: In simple words, after five years, an old health history cannot be used as an excuse called non disclosure.
visual: The CASHLESS DENIED stamp from H005 slides under the clause and is struck through in gold.

en: There is only one exception. Proven fraud. Not a small mistake, not a forgotten fever. Fraud that the company has to establish.
visual: Magnifier on the words 'except for established fraud'.

en: Two honest points. Your normal policy limits and exclusions still apply. And if you change insurer by porting, your years move with you. If you cancel and buy a new policy, the count starts again from zero.
visual: Two cyan cards slide in lower right: LIMITS STILL APPLY · PORT, DON'T CANCEL; real b-roll of a family reading papers at a dining table.
onscreen: PORT, DON'T CANCEL [IRDAI MASTER CIRCULAR | PARA 13 NOTE]

en: Now think about our family at the billing counter. Six years of policy. A rejection letter that says non disclosure. That excuse goes against the IRDAI rule.
visual: Callback: the night lobby shot from H001, the six receipts from H002, the stamp from H005 each flash once; the 60-month ring closes around them.

en: And there is one more rule. A clock.
visual: Clock face materialises over the billing counter footage.

en: When you ask for cashless, the company must decide within one hour. And when the hospital sends the discharge request, the company must give final approval within three hours.
visual: Animated discharge clock: 1-HOUR ring for the cashless request, then a 3-HOUR countdown sweeping in amber.

en: IRDAI says the patient should not be made to wait for discharge. If the approval comes later than three hours, any extra amount the hospital charges for that delay is paid by the insurance company, from its own funds, not by you.
visual: Highlighter on para 16(b) 'borne by the insurer from shareholder's fund'; then real b-roll of a patient in a wheelchair at the hospital exit.
onscreen: DELAY COST · INSURER PAYS [IRDAI MASTER CIRCULAR | PARA 16(b)]

en: Most people never use this rule, because nobody told them it exists.
visual: Slow drift on a hospital corridor clock at night.

en: So, what should you do if your cashless is denied at the counter tonight?
visual: Chapter lower third over the night billing counter footage.

en: Do not shout at the hospital staff. Do not panic. Follow these four steps.
visual: A four-step staircase builds in the lower-left corner, step 1 lit (persistent accent through the chapter).

en: Step one. Collect your papers before you leave.
visual: Step 1 lights; real b-roll of a hand collecting papers into a file at a counter.

en: If you have to pay the bill yourself, pay it. But before you leave the hospital, ask for copies of these papers.
visual: Real b-roll: a payment at a hospital counter (card or UPI).

en: The discharge summary. The final bill with full break up. All test reports and pharmacy bills. And the cashless denial letter.
visual: A checklist builds as papers drop into a file, one per item (SIMULATION documents).

en: If they said the admission was not needed, ask your treating doctor for a short letter on why it was needed.
visual: Real b-roll: a doctor signing a letter at a desk.

en: Step two. File a reimbursement claim, within the time your policy gives. Usually about thirty days from discharge.
visual: Step 2 lights; SIMULATION insurer claim form on a phone screen; a 30-day calendar strip.
onscreen: 2 · CLAIM REIMBURSEMENT · USUALLY 30 DAYS [CHECK YOUR POLICY WORDING]

en: If they reject it, write to the company's grievance officer. Keep it calm and clear. Give your policy number, claim number and amount. If your policy has crossed five years, quote the moratorium rule.
visual: Animated email draft typing itself (SIMULATION): Subject 'Grievance: claim no. ...', lines for policy no., claim no., amount, 'IRDAI moratorium, para 13'.

en: The company has to reply to your complaint within fourteen days.
visual: A 14-day counter in the corner of the screen.

en: Step three. Register your complaint on Bima Bharosa.
visual: Step 3 lights; credited screen recording of the Bima Bharosa portal home page.

en: If the company ignores you, or sends the same reply again, go to bimabharosa dot irdai dot gov dot in. This is IRDAI's own complaint portal. Your complaint goes to the company, and IRDAI can see it and track it.
visual: Screen recording: the complaint registration page (credited, short excerpt, magnifier on the form fields).

en: And step four. The strongest one. The Insurance Ombudsman.
visual: Step 4 lights brightest; slow push on the CIO website header (credited screen recording).

en: If the company rejects your complaint, or does not reply for thirty days, you do not need to start with a consumer court or an expensive lawyer.
visual: Real b-roll: a court building exterior, then a lawyer's desk; both slide away, replaced by a phone screen.

en: Go to the Insurance Ombudsman website, cioins dot co dot in.
visual: Screen recording: cioins.co.in, cursor on Register Complaint.
pacing: VO_PAUSE 3.0 s after this line (owner's 3 s silence): the 4-step online form plays in full

en: The Ombudsman system was set up by the government, only to settle complaints between policyholders and insurance companies.
visual: Credited title page of the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 under the magnifier.

en: You can file the complaint online. It costs nothing. You can explain your case yourself, without a lawyer. File it within one year of the company's final reply.
visual: Kinetic tags over the online form: FREE · ONLINE · NO LAWYER NEEDED · WITHIN 1 YEAR.

en: Now the good part. In the year twenty twenty four, twenty five, the Ombudsman offices received over thirty two thousand health insurance complaints.
visual: Animated counter climbs to 32,503 over a real photo of an Ombudsman office (if available) or the annual report cover.

en: Out of the cases they settled or decided, about three out of every four went in favour of the policyholder.
visual: BOARD: marker works it out: 9,417 settled + 6,126 awards for policyholder = 15,543 of 20,440 decided → 76%.
onscreen: OUR CALCULATION · 76% [CIO ANNUAL REPORT 2024-25 | STATEMENT H3]

en: And about eight out of ten complaints were closed within three months.
visual: Animated bar: 78.5% of disposed complaints in the 'within 3 months' band.
onscreen: OUR CALCULATION · 8 IN 10 IN 3 MONTHS [CIO ANNUAL REPORT | 2024-25]

en: The Ombudsman can award up to fifty lakh rupees. The award is binding on the insurance company. It must pay within thirty days, or pay a penalty of five thousand rupees for every day of delay, to you.
visual: Highlighter on master circular para 20 (30 days, ₹5,000 per day); cyan counters ₹50 LAKH · 30 DAYS · ₹5,000/DAY.

en: And if you are not happy with the award, you can still go to a consumer court.
visual: Real b-roll: a consumer commission building exterior (credited).

en: That is how you fight a big company. Not with anger. With the rules.
visual: The four steps glow together; slow push on a family walking out of a hospital in daylight.

en: Finally, let us be practical. How do you stop this problem before you even reach a hospital?
visual: Chapter lower third; daylight now (art direction: night → day from this chapter).

en: When you buy or renew health insurance, remember three rules.
visual: Three tabs return, now in cyan.

en: Rule one. Never hide anything in the proposal form. Write it down.
visual: Real b-roll: a hand filling a paper form at a table.

en: If you smoke now and then, if you have mild thyroid or blood pressure, write it clearly in the form.
visual: Macro: pen ticks boxes on a SIMULATION proposal form: tobacco, thyroid, BP.

en: Yes, the company may charge a little extra, or add a waiting period. But once it is written in your form, it cannot later call it non disclosure.
visual: The ticked form gets a cyan DECLARED stamp; a small waiting-period bar appears and then completes.

en: Rule two. Look for a policy with no room rent limit, or stay in a room within your limit.
visual: Real b-roll: a hospital single room; a price tag swings onto the door (SIMULATION).

en: A cheaper policy with a room rent limit of one percent of the cover can look like a saving. But one night in a bigger room can cut a big part of your surgery claim.
visual: BOARD callback: the 5 ÷ 8 maths from H027 flashes, the sixty-thousand cut circled again.

en: Rule three. Ask about a consumables cover.
visual: Real b-roll: gloves, syringes and gauze on a hospital tray.

en: Gloves, masks, syringes and similar items are often not paid by a normal policy. They can be five to fifteen percent of a hospital bill. Many insurers sell an add on cover for this. Check the price before you buy.
visual: Animated bill: the consumables lines highlight in amber, a 5–15% bracket appears beside them.
onscreen: 5–15% OF A BILL [INSURER AND BROKER GUIDES]

en: Remember, you pay for health insurance so your family has peace of mind in its weakest moment.
visual: Real b-roll: a father and son walking slowly in a hospital garden, morning light.

en: Do not let a denial letter scare you. Know the five year rule. Use the Ombudsman. And protect your hard earned savings.
visual: Recap montage: the stamp, the 60-month ring, the 3-hour clock, the four steps, each 1 s.

en: Be smart. Be informed. And always, be practical.
visual: Slow pull out from the family in daylight.
sound: Music swells to the end card

en: If this video helped you, share it with one family member who has health insurance. Subscribe, and ask your questions in the comments.
